claim: 70 participants completed a learning task in which they had to choose one of two stimuli based on the separately estimated magnitudes of win and loss outcomes associated with the stimuli.
source: 70 participants (see Table 1 for demographic information) completed a learning task in which they had to choose one of two stimuli based on the separately estimated magnitudes of win and loss outcomes associated with the stimuli (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of participants and describes the task they completed.

claim: Participants were able to learn the best option to choose in the task, selecting the most highly rewarded option on an average of 71% of trials.
source: Participants were able to learn the best option to choose in the task, selecting the most highly rewarded option on an average of 71% of trials (range 65–74%).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific performance data showing participants' success rate in the task.

claim: The mean age of participants was 29.07 years with a standard deviation of 10.86.
evidence: Table 1 provides demographic data including age statistics.

claim: 69% of participants were female.
source: Gender 69% Female
evidence: Table 1 provides demographic data including gender distribution.

claim: An effect of noise was observed, but in the opposite direction to expected, with outcomes influencing choice more when noise was increased.
source: An effect of noise was observed, but in the opposite direction to expected, with outcomes influencing choice more when noise was increased (F(1,696)=4.79, p=0.03).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows a significant effect of noise with F-statistic and p-value, but the direction contradicts predictions.

claim: There was a significant main effect of volatility on learning rates, with a higher learning rate used when volatility was high.
source: Consistent with the analysis of choice data reported above, there was a significant main effect of volatility (Figure 2c–d; F(1,696)=22.2, p<0.001), with a higher learning rate used when volatility was high.
evidence: Statistical analysis of learning rates shows a significant effect of volatility with F-statistic and p-value provided.

claim: There was no main effect of noise on learning rate.
source: There was no main effect of noise (F(1,696)=0.63, p=0.43) on learning rate or outcome valence (F(1,696)=0.15, p=0.7).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows no significant effect of noise on learning rates with F-statistic and p-value provided.

claim: An interaction between volatility and noise on learning rates was significant.
source: An interaction between volatility and noise (F(1,693)=7.74, p=0.006) was also significant.
evidence: Statistical analysis shows a significant interaction effect with F-statistic and p-value provided.

claim: Higher volatility led to a significantly raised learning rate when noise was low.
source: A higher volatility led to a significantly raised learning rate when noise was low (F(1,383)=27.1, p<0.01), with a non-significant increase when noise was high (F(1,311)=1.13, p=0.29).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the interaction shows specific effects under different noise conditions with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Higher noise was associated with a significant increase in learning rate when volatility was low.
source: Higher noise was associated with a non-significant reduction in learning rates when volatility was high (F(1,347)=2.57, p=0.11) but to a significant increase in learning rate when volatility was low (F(1,347)=4.7, p=0.031).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows specific effects of noise under different volatility conditions with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: The Bayesian Observer Model (BOM) adapts as expected, using a higher learning rate both when volatility increases and when noise decreases.
source: As can be seen, the BOM adapts as expected, using a higher learning rate both when volatility increases (F(1,696)=422, p<0.001) and when noise decreases (F(1,696)=21.2, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the BOM's behavior shows significant effects with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Removing the ability of the BOM to adapt to changes in either volatility or noise did not recapitulate the pattern of learning rates observed in participants.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3g–h, neither of these lesions recapitulates the pattern of learning rates observed in participants, with the volatility lesioned model attributing increased volatility to noise and thus decreasing its learning rate during periods of higher volatility (main effect of volatility; F(1,696)=11.9, p<0.001) and the SD-lesioned model treating any form of uncertainty as volatility and thus increasing its learning rate in response to increased noise (main effect of noise; F(1,696)=227, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of lesioned models shows they do not match participant behavior, with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: The degraded BOM more closely recapitulated the learning rates observed in participants, with a significant increase in learning rate in response to increased volatility and no effect of noise.
source: As can be seen from Figure 3i, this relative degrading of the model's representation of uncertainty more closely recapitulated the learning rates observed in participants, with a significant increase in learning rate in response to increased volatility (F(1,696)=59, p<0.001) and no effect of noise (F(1,696)=2.3, p=0.13).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the degraded BOM shows it better matches participant behavior with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Model comparison between the BOM and the RW models based on BIC scores favoured the BOM.
source: Model comparison between the BOM and the RW models based on BIC scores favoured the BOM (mean (SD) for BOM; 235 (54), for complex RL measurement model; 281 (57), for simple RL model; 246 (58)).
evidence: BIC scores are provided for model comparison showing the BOM has lower (better) scores.

claim: The BOM was degraded by reducing the number of bins it used to represent volatility and/or noise, which led to a greater coarsening of the noise than the volatility dimension.
source: The BOM was degraded by reducing the number of bins it used to represent volatility and/or noise, until its behaviour most closely matched that of participants. This process led to a greater coarsening of the noise than the volatility dimension (Figure 4a; F(1,69)=49, p<0.001), with no effect of outcome valence (F(1,69)=0.73, p=0.4), suggesting that the degraded model maintained a generally less precise representation of noise than volatility.
evidence: Statistical analysis shows differential coarsening of noise vs volatility dimensions with F-statistic and p-value provided.

claim: Coarsening the model caused it to miscategorise more trials which the intact BOM had labelled as having high than low noise.
source: Consistent with the greater degradation of the noise dimension, coarsening the model caused it to miscategorise more trials which the intact BOM had labelled as having high than low noise (Figure 4b; F(1,69)=30.7, p<0.01) with no effect of volatility (F(1,69)=1.9, p=0.17) or outcome valence (F(1,69)=0.004, p=0.95).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows differential miscategorization of high vs low noise trials with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: When the degraded BOM miscategorised high noise trials, it tended to label them as having high, rather than low, volatility.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4c, when the degraded BOM miscategorised high noise trials, it tended to label them as having high, rather than low, volatility.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 4c which shows the pattern of miscategorization.

claim: Participants significantly increased their learning rate when the degraded BOM estimated volatility to be high and noise to be low.
source: As can be seen (Figure 4f), participants significantly increased their learning rate when the degraded BOM estimated volatility to be high (F(1,566)=86, p<0.001) and noise to be low (F(1,566)=81, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis using degraded BOM trial labels shows participants respond normatively with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: This normative response to uncertainty was not seen when the labels from the intact rather than the degraded BOM were used.
source: In control analyses, this normative response to uncertainty was not seen when the labels from the intact rather than the degraded BOM were used (Figure 4e), or when the BOM's representation of outcome mean was degraded, rather than its estimates of volatility and noise (supplementary materials).
evidence: The manuscript states that control analyses using intact BOM labels did not show the normative pattern.

claim: Participants' pupils do not adapt normatively to the task block structure, with no main effect of block volatility and an increase of pupil size in response to higher noise.
source: We first show (Figure 5a–c) that participants' pupils do not adapt normatively to the task block structure, with no main effect of block volatility (F(1,1723)=0.002, p=0.9) and an increase of pupil size in response to higher noise (F(1,1723)=13.8 p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of pupil data by task block shows no effect of volatility and opposite effect of noise with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Analysis using the trial labels derived from the degraded model recovered the expected increase in pupil size in response to both raised volatility and reduced noise.
source: In contrast, analysis using the trial labels derived from the degraded model (Figure 5d–f) recovered the expected increase in pupil size in response to both raised volatility (F(1,2067)=105, p<0.001) and reduced noise (F(1,2067)=42.3, p<0.001) suggesting that the model provides a reasonable measure of participants' estimates of these parameters.
evidence: Statistical analysis of pupil data using degraded BOM labels shows normative responses with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: The degraded model was able to account for variance associated with outcome noise that was not explained by the full model.
source: This second level analysis (Figure 5h–i) indicated that the degraded model was able to account for variance associated with outcome noise that was not explained by the full model (F(1,286)=4.1, p=0.04), but did not explain additional variance associated with outcome volatility (F(1,286)=0.1, p=0.75).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows the degraded model explains additional variance in pupil data beyond the intact model with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Humans respond appropriately to changes in volatility irrespective of outcome valence.
source: Previously, we showed that humans respond appropriately to changes in volatility irrespective of outcome valence (Pulcu and Browning, 2017), but there is less evidence of a rational response to noise.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study by the authors showing this effect.

claim: Efficient learning requires estimation of, and adaptation to, different forms of uncertainty.
source: Efficient learning requires estimation of, and adaptation to, different forms of uncertainty.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract, drawing on established understanding in the learning literature.

claim: If uncertainty is caused by randomness in outcomes (noise), observed events should have less influence on beliefs.
source: If uncertainty is caused by randomness in outcomes (noise), observed events should have less influence on beliefs, whereas if uncertainty is caused by a change in the process being estimated (volatility) the influence of events should increase.
evidence: This is a normative prediction based on established learning theory principles.

claim: If uncertainty is caused by a change in the process being estimated (volatility) the influence of events should increase.
source: If uncertainty is caused by randomness in outcomes (noise), observed events should have less influence on beliefs, whereas if uncertainty is caused by a change in the process being estimated (volatility) the influence of events should increase.
evidence: This is a normative prediction based on established learning theory principles.

claim: Participants are adapting to estimated noise, but their estimates are imprecise, leading them to misattribute it as volatility and thus to respond inappropriately.
source: Using a Bayesian observer model, we demonstrate that participants are, in fact, adapting to estimated noise, but that their estimates are imprecise, leading them to misattribute it as volatility and thus to respond inappropriately.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the Bayesian observer model analysis of participant behavior.

claim: The normative response to changes in volatility and noise is to use a higher learning rate when volatility is high and/or noise is low.
source: As described above, the normative response to changes in volatility and noise is to use a higher learning rate when volatility is high and/or noise is low (Pulcu and Browning, 2019; Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: This normative prediction is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A large number of studies have found the predicted increase in learning rates in response to higher outcome volatility in human learners.
source: A large number of studies have found the predicted increase in learning rates in response to higher outcome volatility in human learners (Behrens et al., 2007; Behrens et al., 2008; Browning et al., 2015; Gagne et al., 2020; Nassar et al., 2012; Pulcu and Browning, 2017).
evidence: Multiple citations are provided to support this claim about the literature.

claim: Previous studies have described the expected reduction of learning rates when outcome noise is high, but only when the level of noise is explicitly signalled in a task or when it is made unambiguous by virtue of being very much smaller than changes in outcome caused by volatility.
source: Previous studies have described the expected reduction of learning rates when outcome noise is high, but only when the level of noise is explicitly signalled in a task (Diederen and Schultz, 2015), or when it is made unambiguous by virtue of being very much smaller than changes in outcome caused by volatility (Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations are provided to support this characterization of previous findings.

claim: Activity of central modulatory neurotransmitter systems have been argued to represent distinct sources of uncertainty during learning, with central norepinepheric (NE)/locus coeruleus (LC) activity described as signalling changes in the associations (i.e. volatility) and central cholinergic activity representing noise.
source: From a neurobiological perspective, activity of central modulatory neurotransmitter systems have been argued to represent distinct sources of uncertainty during learning, with central norepinepheric (NE)/locus coeruleus (LC) activity described as signalling changes in the associations (i.e. volatility) and central cholinergic activity representing noise (Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: A citation is provided to support this theoretical framework about neurotransmitter systems.

claim: Electrophysiological measures of LC activity in non-human primates have been shown to correlate with pupil dilation.
source: Electrophysiological measures of LC activity in non-human primates have been shown to correlate with pupil dilation (Joshi et al., 2016), suggesting it may be possible to estimate activity in this system in humans using pupilometry.
evidence: A citation is provided to support this empirical finding.

claim: Studies of human participants report greater pupillary size in volatile relative to stable contexts.
source: Taking this approach, indirect support for this role of the NE system has been provided by studies of human participants that report greater pupillary size in volatile relative to stable contexts (Browning et al., 2015; Nassar et al., 2012; Pulcu and Browning, 2017).
evidence: Citations are provided to support this empirical finding in humans.

claim: The pupil has been reported as being smaller when outcome noise is high.
source: However, the pupil also responds to other learning signals, such as surprise (Browning et al., 2015; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Preuschoff et al., 2011) and has been reported as being smaller when outcome noise is high (Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations are provided to support this empirical finding.

claim: Neuroimaging evidence suggests an association between activity in other central neurotransmitter nuclei, including the cholinergic basal forebrain, and pupil dilation.
source: Neuroimaging evidence suggests an association between activity in other central neurotransmitter nuclei, including the cholinergic basal forebrain, and pupil dilation (de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: A citation is provided to support this neuroimaging finding.

claim: The pupillary signal may reflect a more general belief updating process rather than a specific volatility signal.
source: Overall, this suggests that the pupillary signal may reflect a more general belief updating process (O'Reilly et al., 2013) rather than a specific volatility signal and thus that, like learning rates, pupil size should increase when noise is reduced as well as when volatility is increased.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and leads to a prediction.

claim: Pupil size should increase when noise is reduced as well as when volatility is increased.
source: Overall, this suggests that the pupillary signal may reflect a more general belief updating process (O'Reilly et al., 2013) rather than a specific volatility signal and thus that, like learning rates, pupil size should increase when noise is reduced as well as when volatility is increased.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the interpretation of previous findings.

claim: The study was approved by the University of Oxford Central Research Ethics Committee (R49753/RE001).
source: The study was approved by the University of Oxford Central Research Ethics Committee (R49753/RE001).
evidence: The manuscript states the ethical approval details.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All participants provided written informed consent to take part in the study, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: The manuscript states the consent procedure.

claim: The task consisted of six blocks of sixty trials each.
source: The task consisted of six blocks of sixty trials each.
evidence: The manuscript describes the task structure.

claim: The volatility and noise of the two outcomes varied independently between blocks with different shapes used in each block.
source: The volatility and noise of the two outcomes varied independently between blocks with different shapes used in each block.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: Participants had to distinguish whether variability in the outcomes is caused by volatility or noise from the temporal structure of the outcomes rather than the size of changes in magnitude.
source: As can be seen, blocks with high volatility and low noise (top left), and those with low volatility and high noise (bottom right), present participants with a similar range of magnitudes. Participants, therefore, have to distinguish whether variability in the outcomes is caused by volatility or noise from the temporal structure of the outcomes rather than the size of changes in magnitude (cf. Diederen and Schultz, 2015; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of the task, with citations to contrast with other approaches.

claim: For both win and loss outcomes, learning rates should be increased when volatility is high and when noise is low.
source: Panel (d) shows the expected adaptation of learning rates in response to the manipulation of volatility and noise; for both win and loss outcomes, learning rates should be increased when volatility is high and when noise is low.
evidence: This is stated as the normative prediction for the task.

claim: A previous study on behavioural response to changes in volatility reported an effect size of d=0.7.
source: A previous study (Pulcu and Browning, 2017) on behavioural response to changes in volatility reported an effect size of d=0.7.
evidence: A citation is provided to support this effect size from a previous study.

claim: The sample size was sufficient to detect an effect size of d=0.35 with 80% power.
source: As the effect size of a noise manipulation was not clear, we recruited a sample size sufficient to detect an effect size of half this value (d=0.35) with 80% power.
evidence: The manuscript describes the power analysis used to determine sample size.

claim: Participants were excluded from the study if they had any psychological or neurological disorders or were currently on psychotropic medication.
source: Participants were excluded from the study if they had any psychological or neurological disorders or were currently on psychotropic medication.
evidence: The manuscript states the exclusion criteria.

claim: No exclusion criteria related to task performance were used.
source: No exclusion criteria related to task performance were used.
evidence: The manuscript states that performance-based exclusions were not applied.

claim: Participants attempted to accumulate as much money as possible by learning the likely magnitude of the wins and losses associated with each shape and using this information to guide their choice.
source: Participants attempted to accumulate as much money as possible by learning the likely magnitude of the wins and losses associated with each shape and using this information to guide their choice.
evidence: The manuscript describes the task instructions and goal.

claim: Participants were informed that the unshaded area of each bar was the amount associated with the unchosen option.
source: Participants were informed that the unshaded area of each bar was the amount associated with the unchosen option.
evidence: The manuscript describes what information was provided to participants.

claim: On each trial, participants knew how much they had won/lost and how much they would have won/lost if they had chosen the other option.
source: Thus, on each trial, participants knew how much they had won/lost and how much they would have won/lost if they had chosen the other option.
evidence: The manuscript describes the feedback provided to participants.

claim: Participants were informed that the task would be split into six blocks, that they had to learn which was the best option to choose, and that this option may change over time.
source: Participants were informed that the task would be split into six blocks, that they had to learn which was the best option to choose, and that this option may change over time.
evidence: The manuscript describes the instructions given to participants.

claim: Participants were not informed about the different forms of uncertainty being investigated or of the underlying structure of the task.
source: They were not informed about the different forms of uncertainty we were investigating or of the underlying structure of the task (that uncertainty varied between blocks).
evidence: The manuscript states what information was withheld from participants.

claim: When volatility was low, the mean of the Gaussian distribution remained constant.
source: When volatility was low, the mean of the Gaussian distribution remained constant, when volatility was high, the mean changed between 25–40, and 60–75 every 9–15 trials.
evidence: The manuscript describes how volatility was manipulated in the task.

claim: When volatility was high, the mean changed between 25–40, and 60–75 every 9–15 trials.
source: When volatility was low, the mean of the Gaussian distribution remained constant, when volatility was high, the mean changed between 25–40, and 60–75 every 9–15 trials.
evidence: The manuscript describes how volatility was manipulated in the task.

claim: When noise was low, the standard deviation of the Gaussian was set to 5, whereas when noise was high, the standard deviation was 35.
source: When noise was low, the standard deviation of the Gaussian was set to 5, whereas when noise was high, the standard deviation was 35.
evidence: The manuscript describes how noise was manipulated in the task.

claim: These schedules resulted in similar ranges of outcome magnitudes for periods of high noise and high volatility.
source: As can be seen from Figure 1b, these schedules resulted in similar ranges of outcome magnitudes for periods of high noise and high volatility.
evidence: The manuscript states this and references Figure 1b which shows the outcome schedules.

claim: The first block for every participant had high volatility and low noise for both win and loss outcomes and was used to familiarise participants with the task.
source: The first block for every participant had high volatility and low noise for both win and loss outcomes and was used to familiarise participants with the task.
evidence: The manuscript describes the purpose of the first block.

claim: Choices from the first block were not used in the analyses presented.
source: Choices from this block were not used in the analyses presented (although including them does not alter the reported pattern of results).
evidence: The manuscript states which data were excluded from analysis.

claim: At the end of the experiment, participants were paid one-fifth of their total winnings, plus a £15 baseline rate for turning up to take part.
source: At the end of the experiment, participants were paid one-fifth of their total winnings, plus a £15 baseline rate for turning up to take part.
evidence: The manuscript describes the payment structure.

claim: Pupillometry data was collected for 36 of the 70 participants.
source: Pupillometry data was collected for 36 of the 70 participants.
evidence: The manuscript states how many participants had pupillometry data collected.

claim: The testing session lasted approximately 70 min per participant.
source: The testing session lasted approximately 70 min per participant.
evidence: The manuscript provides the duration of the testing session.

claim: The best fitting RL model included separate learning rates for win and loss outcomes.
source: The best fitting RL model included separate learning rates for win and loss outcomes allowing estimation of the degree to which participants adjusted these learning rates in response to the block-wise changes in outcome volatility and noise (see Supplementary materials and methods for model comparison and selection analyses).
evidence: The manuscript states which model was selected based on model comparison.

claim: The estimated choice inverse temperature was lower when the noise of either outcome was higher.
source: The estimated choice inverse temperature was lower when the noise of either outcome was higher (win: F(1,345)=25.3, p<0.001; loss: F(1,345)=55.7, p<0.001) and was not affected by outcome volatility (p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows effects of noise on inverse temperature with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Including inverse temperature as a covariate in the analysis of participant learning rates did not influence the reported pattern of results.
source: Including inverse temperature as a covariate in the analysis of participant learning rates did not influence the reported pattern of results.
evidence: The manuscript reports a control analysis showing robustness of the main findings.

claim: The BOM was provided with the win and loss outcomes for each trial, across all trials in the task.
source: The BOM was provided with the win and loss outcomes (as values between 0 and 1) for each trial, across all trials in the task (excluding the first practice block, although including this did not alter the pattern of results).
evidence: The manuscript describes what data was provided to the BOM.

claim: The BOM treated the two outcomes as independent.
source: It treated the two outcomes as independent (i.e. the win outcome did not influence estimates for the loss outcome and vice versa) and transformed the outcomes to the infinite real line using the logistic transform before estimating the posterior probability (Pulcu et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript describes how the BOM processed the outcomes.

claim: At the start of each task block, the BOM's belief about the actual magnitude associated with the two new shapes was reset, while maintaining its belief about the overall volatility and noise of the outcomes.
source: This was dealt with in the BOM by flattening the mu dimension of the joint probability distribution at the start of each trial (i.e. replacing the values of the mean dimension, with the average of the joint distribution across this dimension). The effect of this is to reset the model's belief about the actual magnitude associated with the two new shapes, while maintaining its belief about the overall volatility and noise of the outcomes.
evidence: The manuscript describes how the BOM handled block transitions.

claim: The number of active latent states was used as an estimate of volatility in the latent-state model.
source: The number of active latent states was used as an estimate of volatility, the log of the model's expected value for the square of the prediction error was used as an estimate of noise.
evidence: The manuscript describes how volatility and noise were estimated from the latent-state model.

claim: The latent-state model replicates the increased learning rate in high volatility blocks demonstrated by participants.
source: As can be seen, it replicates the increased learning rate in high volatility blocks demonstrated by participants (F(1,696)=9.98, p=0.001), however, unlike participants, it significantly increases its learning rate in response to noise (F(1,696)=100, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of the latent-state model shows it captures some but not all aspects of participant behavior with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Using the labels for high/low volatility and noise derived from the latent-state model does not rescue normative behaviour in participants.
source: Using the labels for high/low volatility and noise derived from the latent-state model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) does not rescue normative behaviour in participants. Participants employ a higher learning rate in trials the model considers to have low relative to high volatility (F(1,556)=7, p=0.008), with no effect of noise (F(1,556)=3.1, p=0.08).
evidence: Statistical analysis shows the latent-state model does not explain participant behavior in the same way as the degraded BOM with F-statistics and p-values provided.

claim: Eye blinks were identified using the built-in filter of the Eyelink system and were removed from the data.
source: Eye blinks were identified using the built-in filter of the Eyelink system and were removed from the data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the preprocessing steps for pupillometry data.

claim: A linear interpolation was implemented for all missing data points (including blinks).
source: A linear interpolation was implemented for all missing data points (including blinks).
evidence: The manuscript describes the preprocessing steps for pupillometry data.

claim: Individual trials were excluded from the pupilometry analysis if more than 50% of the data from the outcome period had been interpolated.
source: Individual trials were excluded from the pupilometry analysis if more than 50% of the data from the outcome period had been interpolated (mean = 6.7% of trials) (Browning et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the exclusion criteria for pupillometry trials.

claim: The first five trials from each block were not used in the pupillometry analysis as initial pupil adaptation can occur in response to luminance changes in this period.
source: The first five trials from each block were not used in the analysis as initial pupil adaptation can occur in response to luminance changes in this period (Browning et al., 2015; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes exclusion criteria with citations supporting the rationale.

claim: Learning rates were transformed to the infinite real line using a logistic transform before analyses.
source: Learning rates were transformed to the infinite real line using a logistic transform before analyses (untransformed data are displayed in figures for ease of interpretation).
evidence: The manuscript describes the data transformation applied before statistical analysis.

claim: The normality of the distribution of the residuals of the LME analyses was checked both visually and with a one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
source: The normality of the distribution of the residuals of the LME analyses was checked both visually and with a one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical checks performed.

claim: Human learners are relatively insensitive to changes in outcome noise.
source: In conclusion, human learners adapt rationally to estimates of the volatility and noise of experienced outcomes. However, these estimates are approximate leading to a relative insensitivity to outcome noise.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper based on the experimental findings.

claim: Participants respond appropriately to a relatively coarse estimation of the level of noise, that led to its misattribution as volatility.
source: Using a degraded BOM to characterise participants' behaviour suggested that they responded appropriately to a relatively coarse estimation of the level of noise, that led to its misattribution as volatility.
evidence: This is a key finding from the degraded BOM analysis.

claim: Human learners are able to adapt to the statistical properties of their environment, but during this process, they make internally consistent errors.
source: These results illustrate that human learners are able to adapt to the statistical properties of their environment, but during this process, they make internally consistent errors, utilising higher learning rates as a result of misattributing environmental noise as volatility which also leads to suboptimal choice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Misattributing environmental noise as volatility leads to suboptimal choice.
source: These results illustrate that human learners are able to adapt to the statistical properties of their environment, but during this process, they make internally consistent errors, utilising higher learning rates as a result of misattributing environmental noise as volatility which also leads to suboptimal choice.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the misattribution observed in the study.

claim: The absence of a normative response to blockwise changes in noise is at odds with previous work which has described a reduction in learning rates during periods of high noise.
source: The absence of a normative response to blockwise changes in noise is at odds with previous work which has described a reduction in learning rates during periods of high noise (Diederen and Schultz, 2015; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript contrasts the current findings with previous literature, citing specific studies.

claim: In previous work, the level of noise was either explicitly presented to participants or was made unambiguous by being very different from changes caused by volatility.
source: However, in this previous work the level of noise was either explicitly presented to participants (as a bar on screen representing the standard deviation of the generative process in Diederen & Schultz) or was made unambiguous by being very different from changes caused by volatility (in Nassar et al, noise was generated using an SD of 5 or 10, while the average change due to volatility was 100).
evidence: The manuscript describes key differences between the current study and previous work.

claim: In the absence of unambiguous differences between outcomes caused by volatility and those caused by noise, participants' ability to estimate and/or adapt to changes in noise is reduced.
source: Our behavioural results suggest that, in the absence of unambiguous differences between outcomes caused by volatility and those caused by noise, participants' ability to estimate and/or adapt to changes in noise is reduced.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the current results with previous findings.

claim: A recent study reported that participants do not adjust their choice or estimated confidence in response to variability in the orientation of arrays of visual gratings.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that participants do not adjust their choice or estimated confidence in response to variability in the orientation of arrays of visual gratings (Herce Castañón et al., 2019), suggesting that an insensitivity to outcome noise may be a general feature of human decision making, rather than a specific component of learning.
evidence: A citation is provided to support this related finding in a different domain.

claim: An insensitivity to outcome noise may be a general feature of human decision making, rather than a specific component of learning.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that participants do not adjust their choice or estimated confidence in response to variability in the orientation of arrays of visual gratings (Herce Castañón et al., 2019), suggesting that an insensitivity to outcome noise may be a general feature of human decision making, rather than a specific component of learning.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited study and the current findings.

claim: Noise fundamentally limits the reliability of information.
source: Noise fundamentally limits the reliability of information (MacKay, 2003) and ignoring it has a clear detrimental impact on inference (Figure 3h), causing agents to be unnecessarily influenced by chance events (Pulcu and Browning, 2019).
evidence: A citation is provided to support this general principle about information theory.

claim: Ignoring noise has a clear detrimental impact on inference, causing agents to be unnecessarily influenced by chance events.
source: Noise fundamentally limits the reliability of information (MacKay, 2003) and ignoring it has a clear detrimental impact on inference (Figure 3h), causing agents to be unnecessarily influenced by chance events (Pulcu and Browning, 2019).
evidence: Citations are provided and Figure 3h is referenced to support this claim.

claim: There is evidence that human learners can respond normatively when the level of noise is unambiguous.
source: It would, therefore, be surprising if human learners were completely insensitive to this process, particularly given evidence that they can respond normatively when the level of noise is unambiguous (Diederen and Schultz, 2015; Nassar et al., 2010; Nassar et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations are provided to support this claim about human learning capabilities.

claim: Participants' pupil size covaries in the expected direction with the degraded BOM's estimated levels of both volatility and noise.
source: The finding that participants' pupil size covaries in the expected direction with the degraded BOM's estimated levels of both volatility and noise provides some reassurance that the model is capturing the dynamics of participants' uncertainty estimates.
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the degraded BOM based on pupillometry data.

claim: The pupillometry signal reflects general belief updating rather than specifically volatility.
source: More generally, the presence of both volatility and noise signals in this data, indicate that, as suggested previously (Nassar et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013), the pupillometry signal reflects general belief updating rather than specifically volatility.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the current data and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The BOM was developed as an algorithmic description of how the learning task may be solved.
source: However, the BOM described here was developed as an algorithmic description of how the learning task may be solved. As far as we are aware, there is little evidence that it accurately describes the cognitive or neural implementation of uncertainty estimation.
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the intended role and limitations of the BOM.

claim: There is little evidence that the BOM accurately describes the cognitive or neural implementation of uncertainty estimation.
source: However, the BOM described here was developed as an algorithmic description of how the learning task may be solved. As far as we are aware, there is little evidence that it accurately describes the cognitive or neural implementation of uncertainty estimation.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: Alternative algorithmic approaches to the general problem of uncertainty estimation have been described.
source: Alternative algorithmic approaches to the general problem of uncertainty estimation have been described (Kalman, 1960; Nassar et al., 2010; Piray and Daw, 2021; Pulcu and Browning, 2019), including simpler approaches that avoid computationally expensive representations of multi-dimensional distributions (Kalman, 1960; Nassar et al., 2010) and which, therefore, may be more likely implementational candidates.
evidence: Citations are provided to support the existence of alternative modeling approaches.

claim: The current results indicate that human learners are relatively insensitive to changes in outcome noise, but do not specify the lower level mechanisms that determine this effect.
source: In other words, the current results indicate that human learners are relatively insensitive to changes in outcome noise, but do not specify the lower level mechanisms that determine this effect.
evidence: This is a summary statement about what the study does and does not reveal.

claim: Previous work examining the neural representations of uncertainty has tended to report correlations between brain activity and some task-based estimate of one form of uncertainty at a time.
source: Previous work examining the neural representations of uncertainty has tended to report correlations between brain activity and some task-based estimate of one form of uncertainty at a time (Behrens et al., 2007; Walker et al., 2020; Walker et al., 2023).
evidence: Citations are provided to characterize the approach of previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Signal-correlation is the degree to which different neurons represent similar external quantities.
source: Specifically, signal-correlation, the degree to which different neurons represent similar external quantities (required to track volatility) is distinguished from, and often limited by, noise-correlation, the degree to which the activity of different neurons covaries independently of these external quantities.
evidence: This is a definition from the neuronal decoding literature.

claim: Noise-correlation is the degree to which the activity of different neurons covaries independently of external quantities.
source: Specifically, signal-correlation, the degree to which different neurons represent similar external quantities (required to track volatility) is distinguished from, and often limited by, noise-correlation, the degree to which the activity of different neurons covaries independently of these external quantities.
evidence: This is a definition from the neuronal decoding literature.

claim: Distinct behavioural and physiological responses to the two forms of uncertainty suggest that separable neural representations of uncertainty are maintained.
source: While the current study clearly cannot adjudicate on the neural representation of these processes, our finding of distinct behavioural and physiological responses to the two forms of uncertainty, does suggest that separable neural representations of uncertainty are maintained.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral and physiological findings.

claim: The reinforcement learning model used to measure learning rates in separate blocks does not achieve the goal of accounting for participants' learning adaptation in response to volatility and noise.
source: Of note, the reinforcement learning model used to measure learning rates in separate blocks does not achieve this goal—as this model is fitted separately to each block rather than adapting between blocks (NB the simple reinforcement learning model that is fitted across all blocks does not capture participant behaviour, see supplementary information).
evidence: The manuscript clarifies the limitations of the measurement model.
